newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Ex-CIA chief says U.S. too slow cutting warheads.
newsitem.headline: Ex-CIA chief says U.S. too slow cutting warheads.

text.p: Former CIA chief Adm. Stansfield Turner on Wednesday said the United States and Russia had far more nuclear warheads than they could possibly use and arms control was in trouble.
He said that during his tenure as Central Intelligence Agency director from 1977 to 1981 he commissioned studies that clearly indicated "we had excess numbers of nuclear weapons."
But Turner told a news conference he had difficulty getting those studies to surface in President Jimmy Carter's administration "because we were starting to build more nuclear weapons."

"As an admiral I saw little usefulness for them and that we had already more than we could possibly use," he said, adding that many of the war plans were unrealistic. He was speaking on the sidelines of an annual review meeting of states that signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Turner said the recent agreement between Russia and the United States in Helsinki did not go far enough to rid the world of an estimated 36,000 stockpiled warheads.

"Helsinki slowed the process down," he said, because it would take until 2008 to fulfil the cuts. "I think this is an indication that the overall arms control process, which has been moving very slowly, is in real trouble."

U.S. and Russian proposals at a summit in Helsinki in March, if ratified, would reduce deployed long-range warheads to 2,000-2,500 for each side by the end of 2007. Instead Turner proposed a "strategic escrow" plan that would remove warheads from operational weapons and place them in storage under observation.

The United States, for example, could start with 1,000 warheads and then wait for the Russians to reciprocate, he said, adding that in just a few years this process could take both sides well below the Helsinki objectives.

"The risk for everyone would be minimal as no one would be giving up weapons," he said. "The powers with nuclear weapons in escrow would checkmate any would-be nuclear aggressor by reassembling some of their weapons."
